candidates.statement: The deﬁnition of test sequence and therefore of the categories LexR(D, A) and MLexR(D, A) it is not completely equivalent to the one in [Ton20, Def 4.3]. As discussed in the proof of the next Theorem the two notions agree when D generates QCoh(X): functors left exact in the sense of [Ton20] are automatically left exact in our sense. In [Ton20] we were looking for a minimal collection of test sequences which make results like the one below true under the assumption that D generates QCoh(X). In this paper instead we will deal with more general subcategories D and therefore this notion of test sequence seems more precise.

Let X be a quasi-compact ﬁbered category over R and D ⊆Vect(X) be a full subcategory that generates QCoh(X). Then Ω∗: QCoh XA →LR(D, A) is fully faithful with essential image LexR(D, A) and it has an exact left adjoint F∗,D : LR(D, A) →QCoh XA. In particular Ω∗and (F∗,D)| LexR(D,A) are quasi-inverses of each other. Assume that D is a monoidal subcategory of Vect(X). Then the functor Ω∗and F∗,D extends to adjoint functors Ω∗: QAlg XA →MLR(D, A) and A∗,C : MLR(D, A) →QAlg XA. Moreover Ω∗: QAlg(XA) →MLexR(D, A) is an equivalence and (A∗,C)| MLexR(D,A) is a quasi-inverse.

Let A = k[x, y, z] and B = k[x/y, y, z/y] and notice that A ⊆B ⊆Ay ⊆Axy = Bx We deﬁne X as the scheme obtained by gluing Spec Ax and Spec B along Spec Axy. By con- struction there are maps Spec A −V (x, y) = Spec Ax ∪Spec Ay →X f−→Spec A As the ﬁrst map is dominant because Spec Ax ⊆X is open, we obtain that H0(OX ) = A.
